main_question: {"author_id": "need2seegreen", "author_name": "Need2SeeGreen 10 (SoCal)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/need2seegreen", "date": "2021-12-15", "text": "hello all! Just out of curiosity, how come it is (sometimes?) thought that it is best to leave a rose on the bush, until it is past flowering, before using the stem to make a cutting? I would expect that there is some type of plant hormone that makes it bloom -  but how come I want to wait?  Or is it a different substance that enhances the rooting of the cutting?  (I am getting a book out of the library that may shed some light, but I was just wondering what people here think.) I am wondering if I can have the rose inside, and still try to make a cutting. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "fig-insanity", "author_name": "fig_insanity Z7b E TN", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fig-insanity", "date": "2021-12-15", "text": "The reason for using a stem with a fading bloom is that new growth that has *just* flowered is at the right stage of maturity to make a viable cutting. You don't want to make a cutting of material that is either too young, or too mature, or your chances of it rooting are greatly lessened. The fading bloom is just a good indicator or ripeness of the wood immediately below, nothing else. It's a good way for beginners to learn what makes a good cutting. Once you are familiar with the best stage of growth from which to make a cutting, you can use wood from non-blooming wood that has reached the optimum stage of ripeness, from anywhere on the bush.", "images": []}}

None of the roses are super mature, since I've only been in this house 3.5 years, and all are mostly dormant.  I moved all of them to pots (multiple per pot) or some of them went into a raised bed at my mother's house to try to keep them through winter until it is time to get them in the ground at the new place.  Luckily it has been a very warm fall for us in colorado, so I was able to dig them. title: Effed-up kitchen counter install — whose fault is this? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "larahale", "author_name": "larahale", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/larahale", "date": "2021-12-15", "text": "Apologies in advance: This is half venting, and half asking for advice. We are in the midst of updating our 1955 midcentury modern home, retaining and restoring as many original details as possible\u2014including the kitchen cabinets. We hired a local countertop fabricator to replace the 80s laminate the previous owners had installed with quartz. The same owners also had installed a 36\" cooktop over a  30\" floor cabinet, and had cut into the interior of the drawer beside that cabinet in order to accommodate the too-large cooktop. When the sales reps came to our home to give an estimate, I pointed this out to them\u2014remarking on the stupid thing the previous owners had done to the drawer\u2014and told them that we had ordered a new cooktop that was 30\", the proper size for the cabinet. They actually insisted that they would not send the template maker out to do the official measurements until our new sink and cooktop had arrived he could physically look at them to ensure he got the precise measurements and angles he needed to create the template. When the template maker arrived, he set about doing his thing, only occasionally popping up his head to ask us a question. The template was sent over that evening with all the details like overhang, material, color, edge shape, etc. as well simple drawings and their terms and conditions. It all looked right to us, so we signed and waited to hear from them on the install. When the pieces were installed two weeks later, there were several little issues with the quality of the work they'd done, including one counter having a slightly deeper overhang than the others. But the one glaring error is that THEY DID NOT CENTER THE COOKTOP OVER THE CABINET BELOW. (photo attached) When we reached out to office, they said they'd check into it and then sent us an email to say that they had placed the new 30\" cooktop exactly where the old inappropriately sized 36\" one was, based on the center of the old countertop. They told us that it is their \"policy\" to place new appliances in the exact position of the old appliances in retrofitted designs. (No such \"policy\" was ever stated to us, nor is it in the template document.) They argue that, if we wanted the new 30\" cooktop to be centered over the 30\" cabinet below, it was our responsibility to specifically tell them that. Our position is that it is standard practice\u2014not to mention common sense\u2014to center a cooktop over the cooktop cabinet and that we had absolutely no reason to think that professional installers would need to be told this. Also, if that is their \"policy,\" why was it not mentioned at any point during the process\u2014when the estimators came, when the template maker came, when the template was sent for sign off? All you have to do is scroll through Houzz to see is *extremely* unusual that anyone would ever place a cooktop off-center of the cabinet below\u2014in such a rare, specific case, would you not make a special point of telling the client it would be off-center and asking if that was their preference?? We believe this entirely their fault; the templater/fabricator messed up and they don't want to admit it. They are not willing to redo the work at their expense, and they are not even offering a discount if we were willing to pay them to correct their mistake. We've been arguing this point with them for more than a month now (we paid half up front and have been withholding the balance pending resolution), and if anything they are digging their heels in deeper each time. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "lakeaffect-gw", "author_name": "lakeaffect_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lakeaffect-gw", "date": "2021-12-18", "text": "Being from Vermont we never had cornbread stuffing, but I do make it, just not on holidays, cuz, you know, tradition. My stuffing is a lot like my grandmother\u2019s, but I use more veggies and herbs, and she used sausage, which I don\u2019t care for, so don\u2019t use. Saute a head of celery (it\u2019s a head, right?) cut into 1/4\u201d slices and 2 large onions cut similarly in butter and olive oil until soft and translucent. For the last couple of minutes of sauteeing add a large bunch of chopped flat leaf parsley, at least 12 chopped sage leaves, at least 12 sprigs of chopped fresh thyme and two of those wasteful plastic herb packages of chopped fresh summer savory. Let cool. Meanwhile, toast 3 loaves of best quality, dense, chewy (no wonder bread) white, sourdough or wheat bread. I use a mix of all, plus assorted bread leftovers that end up in the freezer. When cooled, tear toasted bread into 1-2\u201d pieces, dump sauteed herbs and veggies into the bowl with the bread and mix well with your hands. Add about 2 cups of homemade or best quality chicken or veggie broth and a cup or so of whole milk, half and half, cream or oat milk and mix together with your hands until it\u2019s uniformly moist, almost spongy, adding more liquid as needed. Taste and salt and pepper to taste, sometimes I add walnuts and that\u2019s also tasty. Butter a large casserole dish and smush the stuffing down well (it compresses nicely) and bake at 300-350 for an hour +-. If you like a crust on top, bake uncovered, if not, use a lidded casserole or cover tightly with tin foil. title: Gästebad mit kleinem Budget aufhübschen - Tips und Ideen gesucht! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "penthesileia", "author_name": "Penthesileia", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/penthesileia", "date": "2021-12-16", "text": "Hallo liebe Community, wir h\u00e4ngen mal wieder an Aufh\u00fcbschungs\u00fcberlegungen und hoffen auf Eure Hilfe und Euren kreativen Input. Sorgenkind ist dieses Mal unser WC im Erdgeschoss, also dem Bereich, in dem wir uns tags\u00fcber \u00fcberwiegend aufhalten (hier sind K\u00fcche, Ess- und Wohnbereich sowie das B\u00fcro) und das G\u00e4ste am ehesten benutzen (wenn das WC dann bald  mal T\u00fcren hat ;)  ). Das WC ist aber auch unser Anlaufpunkt, an dem wir nach dem Gassigehen die Schuhe sauber machen und wo Putzeimer gef\u00fcllt und geleert werden. Da nach den Renovierungsma\u00dfnahmen nun das Geld nicht mehr ganz so locker sitzt, wollen wir das WC nicht komplett ummodeln. D.h. Boden und Wandfliesen sollen bleiben. Die Bodenflie\u00dfen werden wir neu verfugen, weil die Fugen ziemlich siffig und por\u00f6s sind. Der Sp\u00fclkasten und die WCsch\u00fcssel sind schon neu. Das Waschbecken muss weg - das hat seine besten Tage gesehen und ist auch besch\u00e4digt. Wandfarbe ist schnell ge\u00e4ndert, obschon ich die Farbe eigentlich ganz gut finde (die habe ich eigentlich im Schlafzimmer und habe aus Mangel an besseren Ideen einfach das WC auch so gestrichen). Der Spiegel muss nicht unbedingt bleiben. Der war schon vorhanden und beim Umzug stellte sich heraus, dass er wundersamerweise genau dorthin passt und wir sonst nirgends Verwendung f\u00fcr ihn haben, weshalb wir ihn kurzerhand hingeh\u00e4ngt haben. Ich finde, dass die gro\u00dfe Spiegelfl\u00e4che dem winzigen fensterlosen Raum die Enge nimmt. Die unsch\u00f6ne R\u00fcmpel-Nische zwischen Wand und Kamin w\u00fcrden wir gerne mit einem auf Ma\u00df gefertigten Einbauschrank sinnvoll nutzen und schlie\u00dfen. An der Wand \u00fcber dem WC w\u00fcrden wir gerne Borde anbringen f\u00fcr bspw. Bilder, h\u00fcbsche/g\u00e4stefreundliche Stehr\u00fcmchen, WC-Lekt\u00fcre... Den Boden w\u00fcrde ich gerne freihalten zum einfachen Putzen. Am meisten Kopfzerbrechen bereiten uns Waschbecken / Waschtisch / Toi-papierhalter / Handtuchl\u00f6sung. Wie Ihr auf den Fotos seht, hat der Fliesenleger hier vor Jahren kein Kunstwerk vollbracht (unsch\u00f6ne gro\u00dfe \"L\u00f6cher\" rund um den Z\u00e4hler und Waschbeckenablauf) - daf\u00fcr muss auch eine L\u00f6sung her. Unsere  Idee ist bis jetzt, ein gro\u00dfes, trogartiges Aufsatzwaschbecken auf eine starke wandh\u00e4ngende Konsole (vielleicht aus massiver Eiche mit Bootslack versiegelt?) zu stellen. Eine \u00dcberlegung war, im selben Holz unter dem Waschbecken ein kleines Bord f\u00fcr Ersatz-Toipapier und Handt\u00fccher anzubringen und die \"Fliesenl\u00f6cher\" dahinter mit einer R\u00fcckwand aus dem selben Material zu verdecken. Eine Waschtisch/Unterschrank-L\u00f6sung erscheint uns suboptimal, weil es da schnell eng wird mit den Knien, wenn man auf dem WC sitzt, bzw. man sich \"eingekastet\" f\u00fchlen k\u00f6nnte - wir hatten das schon mit Kartons versucht nachzustellen. Auch denken wir, dass wir den Stauraum unterm Waschbecken nicht ben\u00f6tigen, weil in dem k\u00fcnftigen Einbauschrank genug Platz f\u00fcr all das ist, was wir im WC unterbringen wollen/m\u00fcssen. Unklar sind wir uns, wie die Konsole mit dem Waschbecken am besten passen w\u00fcrde. \u00dcber die ganze Wandl\u00e4nge durchgezogen? K\u00fcrzer? \u00dcberall in der selben Tiefe ggf. sich verj\u00fcngend / schmaler werdend?  Was f\u00fcr ein Waschbecken und was f\u00fcr ein Wasserhahn, die trotz der Trogartigkeit zu unserer WCSch\u00fcssel passen? Wohin dann mit Toipapier-Halter und wo soll das Handtuch hin? title: Bought some new cookware | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bmorepanic", "author_name": "bmorepanic", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bmorepanic", "date": "2021-12-16", "text": "For some reason, decided to take a tour of mid-range makers while doing it.  I am moderately good cook with occasional flashes of brilliant balanced by the occasional fail. Honestly, I had crap.  Some of it I got for free by collecting coupons at the grocery store.  I kept a few things - the huge stainless stockpot I keep in the basement except for turkey time.  One small Italian fry pan.  It has good heat distribution and inertia - good for single person omelet but mediocre for scrambled or individual eggs.  Also kept a 5 qt Sur La Table enameled cast iron braiser - I once jammed a 22 pound spatchcocked turkey in it. To be clear, everything I bought made me a better cook (well, except for \"The Disappointment\").  I hadn't realized how awful my stuff was until I had the opportunity to use something better.  I was stunned.  I am in no way in the price group of all All Clad 3 or all LeCreuset but I understand why one might want better stuff now. FRYING PANS The egg pan - 8\" All Clad essentials.  Gas or Electric but not induction. This was the first pan I bought (Home Goods $10).  Oh my, yes.  Non-stick works well and the pan heats and cools really rapidly.  The coating dents if you look at it wrong but so far, it doesn't affect it's nonstickness. The flat, round griddle-like thing for tortillas and Grilled Cheese.  This replaces the $6 cheapest imusa coma pan that was made from aluminum foil.  SENSARTE Nonstick Crepe Pan (Amazon $33).  Does induction as well as gas & electric.  It has a little bit of an edge with a tiny well all around the rim.  Heats up well, heat is even, dumps heat in a reasonable time.  Tortillas do well as does pan toasting just about anything - including a pile of cheese & jalapeno.  Fits two grilled sands.  I should try pan seared veg on it.  I hope it has a long lifespan. Fish for dinner - 10\" sear-fry.  Cuisinart Multiclad Pro tri-ply non-stick saute.  Exterior is Tri-ply, Induction Gas Electric.  About $45 with a lid.  Even heat - takes a while to heat up and retains heat well - a characteristic of all heayweight tri-plys.  Sears really well.  I may someday get the higher sided 5 quart, no coating.  The handle is a little odd and that can be uncomfortable.  I \"fixed\" it by changing my grip a little after I noticed that it was fine in my left hand. Big saute - 12\" (get ready for it) Food Ninja Foodie Neverstick Premium Everyday pan with a lid.  About $80.  Induction, Gas, Electric.  Be careful about the label, the not premium ones aren't as nice.  Oven safe - even with the lid - up to 500 F.  Insanely even temperatures after preheating.  Stays hot longer. POTS Cuisinart 1 qt French tri-ply - really nice, heavy weight but tiny.  Needs care with 12 oz can of soup, About $55 with a lid.  Induction, Gas, Electric. Cuisinart 2 qt  Multiclad Pro.  About $50 with a lid.  This is a tiny bit lighter than a French version and also wider and shorter.  When the pots start getting big, this is my personal preference.  Really can contain 2 quarts.  Same minor handle issue. The Disappointment. Breville Thermal Pro Hard Anodized Nonstick Saucier 2.5 qt.  Sigh!  About $85 with a lid.  Induction, gas or electric. The practical size is about 1.5 quart (a few curse words deleted).  It's sort of inverted bell shaped - the top wings out and then chokes inward before flaring out again - just enough to make it a little bit difficult to stir.  It's induction capable by a small plate imbedded in the bottom.  Using with gas, the plate is enough to change the characteristics of how the pan heats.  The sides curve up from the plate and get hotter than the plate does.  So its hard to stir and has uneven heating in a Saucier.   Probably works better on induction.  Can do oven up to 500F. Cuisinart Enameled Cast Iron 3 qt covered  casserole.  Induction, gas or electric.  Home Goods for $25 if they still have any.  It's taller and narrower than most casserole style pots.  Heats evenly, sears great on it's little bottom.  Interior color is cream (keep it cream with oxiclean).  Of course, it does oven.  It's become my 3 qt go to pot. Hestan Probond try-ply 3 qt soup with lid.  It was on sale and still the most expensive thing I bought at $125.  All those cheers for Nanobond were contagious.  It's less than 1/2 the weight of the cuisinart cast iron,  but equal performance with a bigger bottom - UNLESS you want to simmer for a long time.  Then, you might need to add a simmer plate.  Is it a really good tri-ply?  You betcha.  Is it perfect?  The handles are a little small. Tramontina 5 qt casserole with lid - a.k.a pasta water.  We had a very small turkey and it did well as a stock pot too.  It sears well and did a good job at keeping a constant, pretty even temperature.  It doesn't have a rolled edge, so pouring is difficult. It's fun being able to rely on your stuff to keep an even temp when you walk away from it for a little while.  I'm still looking for a wok.", "images": []}

title: Grout line in bad place, need advice | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lk97", "author_name": "Logan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lk97", "date": "2021-12-16", "text": "Working on my first ever tiling project, our kitchen backsplash. We are using a polished marble tile with a companion accent piece. I did a small section of the kitchen (not shown in any of the pictures) in order to get the hang of it before doing the main area. That side area has been completed and grouted although not caulked yet. I have since moved on to doing the main backsplash area. In designing the layout, we decided to end the backsplash where the upper cabinet ends since we didn't like the idea at all of continuing past. We also decided to continue the backsplash all the way up the wall around the window. Basically I had 3 areas to balance to try to not have any slivers: the end, around the window, and the back corner. If I left a grout line running between the window trim and the upper cabinets, it resulted in a sliver of less than an inch both on the end and in the back corner. So I tried shifting it around to get the best possible balance. What I decided on was to conceal the grout lines entirely under the window trim and (essentially) behind the cabinets. This meant getting 2.5\" trim instead of 2.25\" in order to barely cover it around the window. This way it would have the appearance of full pieces of tile around the window without any awkward pieces or grout lines. By doing that, the end tiles would be roughly 4.75\" and 1.75\" which looks fine to me. The back corner would admittedly have slivers but its hidden so that took lowest priority. I saw this layout as the best compromise. The day I started tiling I meant to check one final time to make sure all 4 grout lines that were in the area would fall underneath either the cabinets or the window trim. I checked 3 and then I believe started working on something else and never went back to check the last, which proved to be a big mistake. So after I had started tiling I realized I somehow ended up with a grout line in a horrible spot along the right cabinet. I don't exactly know how I screwed it up - my cuts were just as I wanted them and I think I must of just assumed that grout line would fall \"behind\" the cabinet. I'm really not sure.        The center of the grout line is about 3/16\" from the edge of the cabinet. Tearing the tile off and redoing it is not an option. What are my options otherwise? title: Transplanting wild American holly trees | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jason-carlton26", "author_name": "Jason, zone 7A, near Greensboro NC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jason-carlton26", "date": "2021-12-16", "text": "I have a TON of wild American holly trees growing throughout my property, and I'd like to move them around to more strategic areas that could use evergreens. Last year I transplanted 10 of them, ranging in height from 2 to 7'. Only one of them survived :-( I made a point to dig up as much soil as possible, and put them in areas with similar sun to what they'd been getting. But still, 9 out of 10 just didn't like it. Which is weird, seeing as how they seem to take root anywhere the wind blows... except for where I want them!!! LOL Any other suggestions on how to successfully move them?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "nandina-gw", "author_name": "nandina", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nandina-gw", "date": "2021-12-17", "text": "Jason, From years of experience with most varieties of Holly I suggest you do the following. Select and tag the young trees you wish to move. This is the perfect time of year for the next step before the snow falls. Using a transplanting shovel, root prune around each young plant about 12 \" from the trunk. Make those cuts straight down....do not try to lift the trees in any manner. Next spring, early March, begin the transplanting project which is pretty standard. Plan to dig and replant each little tree one at a time, placing the dug root ball on a section of burlap or old blanket. At this point I like to have a strong-back companion and together we will walk the tree to its new location gently, decide how large a hole to dig and settle it in firmly. I do not like to   leave them sitting in a deep, concave water collecting area, especially if you have clay soil. Everything in moderation. If all the leaves fall off, don't give up. Wait and observe the green buds that may form close to the trunk. If this happens prune just ahead of those buds and the tree will recover and grow normally.", "images": []}}

When we renovated, we chose the Kalia Surfer faucet in stainless because it's pretty and because we had a credit to use at the appliance store, but it broke and won't swivel correctly and we hate it. Kalia did send a replacement, but they have not fixed the design flaw so it's just going to break again. So, new faucet, I guess!  (Don't buy this faucet.) But in the past we've had a gooseneck faucet with the handle on the side and it was great, so not a dealbreaker. I do plan to stick with stainless and single-hole and with a pull-out or pull-down. title: Asbestos help please | Houzz Forum

I never thought about asbestos before my friend died. Does this sound like an exposure to worry about? If not could somebody please explain to me why not. I buy a few sets of those soft white LED lights for one of our large windows, and a small battery set for the kitchen door window or twig wreath. It looks great with large colored lights. Nice to see when arriving home. Give some time to turning off any television or news or radio and put on some beautiful music. I have my cooking music CDs (Graceland), but listening to beautiful piano, choral, opera, or jazz is a soothing respite from a crazy world. main_question: {"author_id": "magner68", "author_name": "Marilyn A", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/magner68", "date": "2021-12-18", "text": "how can i easily remove old hard water stains from chrome finishes? ive tried vinegar, bar keepers friend, etc and nothing seems to work. thamks in advance.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "brbyah", "author_name": "loobab", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/brbyah", "date": "2021-12-18", "text": "I take a paper towel soaked in vinegar and wrap it around the shower spigot and then a baggy around the whole thing attached with string or a rubber band and let that sit for several hours. That works best if you do it regularly if you live in a hard water area which I do. CLR (you can buy it in the hardware store or Home Depot ) makes a spray foam that adheres (so it doesn't drip) and you can use that too. Just be careful you don't use anything too strong for too long or you can damage the fixtures. Please invite Joe Corlett into this thread, for sure he has better ideas than I. My water is so hard I can't use bar soap because it makes an icky scum on the bathtub and shower walls, I use glycerin-based liquid soap. I read somewhere that you don't want to spend a fortune on plumbing fixtures for this reason when you have very hard water and you don't have a water softener. On another note, one time I dropped a knife (a super sharp Henckels chef knife) taking it out of the knife block and it cut the spigot, so it (the spigot) had to be replaced. I don't like those magnet strips for knives because having blades exposed, that is just a disaster waiting to happen. What is not in the block is in a drawer with knife shields. There used to be a show on TV that is no longer on with two women from the UK, Kim and Aggie with all sorts of housekeeping tips, \"How Clean is Your House.\" I learned a lot from them, they use a lot of everyday things, you don't need to purchase carts full of proprietary products. Sorry, I went off on a tangent.", "images": []}}

title: Have you ever been offered a promotion you weren’t looking for? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "primdawg", "author_name": "Annette Holbrook(z7a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/primdawg", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "I am at an age where my work life is kind of winding down. My husband and I owned and ran a large dog training and care facility. We sold our place and moved to this vacation town a few years ago. My husband is 16 years older than I so he is already retired. When we moved up here I was retired as well, but that lasted about 6 months. I took a part time job at the local Tractor Supply to keep busy.  Generally a fun job and discounts on all my pet supplies. After only about 2 1/2 months there I got promoted to one of the managers, which I saw as a challenge as I had never worked in retail at all. So I jumped back into full-time and all was good. Unlike a lot of the youngsters there I had no aspirations to take the corprate train to a higher up level in corporate, so was quite fine doing my thing. And then Covid hit. Since TSC is a feed store, it is considered essential and therefore we kept working. However, I am in an area where people don\u2019t believe in precautions and such so we had coworkers constantly out with covid and we had customers who would get nasty with employees about wearing masks or social distancing. We would also get verbal abuse when we were out of products and such. So anyway, I had enough one day and just walked out(I have never done anything like that!) I took a mental health break for about a month and then started looking for work again. I ended up getting hired at an animal hospital to be a front desk rep. A good fit for my animal experience and my prior life as a corprate travel specialist(unlike many of the younger group, I have no trouble talking on the phone lol). So here it is 5+ months in and the supervisor of my department is stepping down. She is not leaving the practice, she just decided she\u2019s not cut out to be a supervisor. One of the parts of the job is dealing with angry customers, which she ended up passing on to me most of the time. She is going to take a position in the kennel and will have minimal contact with the clients. The hospital manager hinted to me a few weeks ago that this was a probability and said she\u2019d like me to take the position. I basically answered by laughing it off. The other 5 people in the department have all been there 4,5,6 years or so. I figured one of them would want the spot for sure. Well, dontcha know, the only person who applied is the one employee the hospital manager absolutely doesn\u2019t want in the job. She is part time because she has kids who are heavily involved in sports and spends all of her free time driving kids to practices and games all over the state, plus she has never worked Saturdays due to this. All that aside, she does know the procedures of the computer system better than anyone, but she breaks policy constantly. I get why the HM doesnt want her to be the supervisor. So this past week, the HM asked me a few times if I was serious about not wanting the position. She told me to name my terms, and that the medical director was in agreement and had approved her offering me the position. By the end of the week I finally told her I\u2019d think about it over the weekend.  So here I sit, trying to decide. On a side note, when this all started, the girl who wants the job asked me point blank if I was going to apply. I told her no, and she asked why(the rest of the team was right there during this exchange) and I told her I\u2019d been there, done that. I was enjoying being a soldier instead of a captain. So I\u2019m pretty sure if I get the job she will be impossible, she does seem to lead the little clique. Another reason the HM wants me for the job, I keep my nose to the grindstone and stay out of office drama. I\u2019m also thinking she may just quit. My friends from the real world(my little core group for over 20 years) are all about me taking the job. But we are always each other\u2019s cheerleaders in these situations lol", "images": []}

title: Do Sempervivum Need a More Organic Soil? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "Sempervivum are alpine rock garden succulents that grow shallow roots in small amounts of soil.   I have had problems getting these to flourish in mixes that do not have some rich organic component.  What kinds of soil mixes have you had success with? With traditional gritty mix, these plants eventually root and grow, but the growth is not abundant without regular synthetic fertilizer.   In studying the soil mixes that professional growers have published online, I could not help but notice that many of them are using clay in the soil mix.   Sempervivivums By Post in the UK is using 3 parts of John Innes #3 soil with one part of grit.   I researched components of the Innes #3 and by my calculations the resulting mix is about 44% clay loam soil.   And this is a container mix! https://sempervivumsbypost.co.uk/pages/advice-sempervivums Sempervivums By Post grows some of the healthiest looking plants I have ever seen in this genus.   The attached photo is their container planting. Another grower I found starts with clay loam soil and adds sand to that. The only thing that I can think of to explain these results is that these plants must like some component of the soil to have a very high CEC, even though they are not heavy feeders (supposedly).   In addition, they seem to like a neutral pH, so they probably are not doing as well in soils with too much peat and bark. Does anyone have insights as to why this genus of succulent does so well in soils with some amount of clay?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/dcd2c1e501be9d1e_2014-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-856346171", "author_name": "John (Zone 5b/6a, IN)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-856346171", "date": "2021-12-20", "text": "I think you kind of answered your own question. When using a version of the gritty mix, I don't think it's reasonable to expect explosive growth if you're not also using regular synthetic fertilizer. While the native environment for semps is most likely nutrient poor, I'd also not expect to see the lush, massive clumps of them in the Alps the same as we do in cultivation. If you want to have your semps grow into large clumps relatively quickly, you'll have to fertilize with every watering most likely. I think this comes down more to, \"the plants need nutrients regularly,\" as opposed to, \"the plants specifically desire clay loam.\"", "images": []}}

title: retaining walls - avoid these mistakes | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bashar-alashhab", "author_name": "Bashar_waronwaste Ashhab", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bashar-alashhab", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "- Building a retaining wall over an easement: Check your easement prior to making any plans as the biggest mistake we find is that customers build retaining walls over easement without encasing the pipes below ground. This is a must as it is part of council rules...due to weight and pressure clay pipes for swage may break! - Timber retaining walls: even though it may be the cheaper option compared to concrete retaining walls, there are specifications which MUST be looked at and planned for. For example, timber retaining wall should ideally retain a height of about 0.6m any more concrete may be the better option for long term, we see this many times, after 5 years customers would call us up to discuss their previous timber retaining wall collapsing over. - Footings for retaining walls: generally N12 or N16 bars utilized in footings. Trying to save money on steel (I know steel has gone up 25% over the past year!) retaining walls are as good as your footings, so do not go cheap on footings.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "gdwright07", "author_name": "gdwright07", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gdwright07", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "Hello! New home owner here. Seeing what I think are weeds popping up in some of our new sod. Can anyone confirm and offer advice on how to resolve. Sod is maybe 3 weeks old.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ec024ec001bf420c_8001-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mishmosh2000", "author_name": "mishmosh2000", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mishmosh2000", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "I would just wait until that sod gets established.  You can easily take care of that and other weeds in the spring with post-emergent spray.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "Ground ivy, Glechoma hederaceae (aka creeping Charlie). This is a perennial weed/groundcover so most likely came with the sod. Because of its stoloniferous nature, it is hard to pull and get very good results so herbicides are recommended. But nighttime temps lower than 45F make herbicides more or less ineffective, so winter is not a great time to attempt control. Wait until spring when things warm up and active growth resumes. In the meantime, feel free to pull to your heart's content!", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "gdwright07", "author_name": "gdwright07", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gdwright07", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "Thanks all!", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "Wait until spring...specifically mid April after the weeds are growing well and the soil has warmed.  Actively growing weeds die better than dormant or sickly weeds.  I would start with Weed-b-Gon Chickweed, Clover, and Oxalis Killer. title: Which Engineered Wood Floor? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "komeht", "author_name": "komeht", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/komeht", "date": "2021-12-19", "text": "OK - we're having to replace our wood floors in our house due to some water infiltration damage on an insurance claim.  And, rather than replace with the existing hickory - we're making a change since the hickory is too yellow, too busy, the planks too narrow. . . The aesthetic of the house is overall scandinavian - clean and modern, on the lighter side. We've decided to go with a white or european oak in a wider plank.  Specifically we're looking at lighter and more natural tones, smooth or very light brushed texture, tighter grain and fewer knots (though some character is welcome of course). After many many hours and samples and going back and forth we have a couple of top contenders. https://villagiowoodfloors.com/product/duna/ https://kentwoodfloors.com/us/our-floors/showroom/brushed-oak-gold-hill The Villagio samples are quite nice with a beautiful but tight grain that shows - I would say the color is blondish with kind of a hey or sand like color - a bit toward more yellow than brown.   The wear layer is 4mm with 5/8\" thickness and the wood is prime AB, polyurethane ao finish.  Planks are a very wide 9.5\".  Appears to be chinese sourced product but I believe is CA section 01350 compliant w/certifications from SCS. The Kentwood is a similar tone that goes more to the brown side than the yellow.  A bit more character - but still quite nice.  Looks like maybe a 3mm wear layer (though Kentwood doesn't seem to say in any of their online materials) on a 9/16\" board and the plank is still wide at 7.5\" instead of 9.5\".  Same polyeurethane ao finish.  I think there is more variation a bit more grain and maybe it's more abc or abcd instead of ab - but again, Kentwood doesn't say. I think they'll both look nice.  The construction seems solid on both with 7 layer ply base.  Not overly concerned with the wear layer as I can't really forsee the need to refinish the floors. Mostly - we're looking for something timeless that will look beautiful no matter what trends are going and mesh with the existing aesthetic.  I'm think I'm drawn a bit more to the Kentwood - but will the construction differences be a concern longterm?", "images": []}

Not sure if it would be important to get a variable speed furnace if have a single stage 16 SEER AC unit. If you have insights on this to help me decide, I would love to hear. Thanks.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mike-home", "author_name": "mike_home", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mike-home", "date": "2021-12-20", "text": "The Legacy models are the low end of the Bryant furnace models. The build quality and features are not as good as the Preferred and Evolution series. I suggest if the budget allows you select a Preferred series furnace to match  your Preferred 126CNA furnace. Your variable speed furnace question is a very good one. The single stage Preferred series is marketed as a variable speed furnace. That is a deceiving label in my opinion. It is really a multi-speed furnace. That means the blower motor can be set to one of several speeds for heating, and another speed for cooling. The two speeds are selected at the time on installation and do not vary. That should be fine for the condenser you have considering. Be aware that the 126CNA condenser is advertised as \"up to 17 SEER\". The SEER rating of the AC system is based on the selected furnace, condenser and its size, and the coil. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-110587825", "author_name": "Epi Phylum", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-110587825", "date": "2022-02-22", "text": "Yes Jasmine hello , i  thought about 20years ago my epiphyllums also had virus , i even was advised to throw them away which i did with some of them at least.  i even thought fungus rust and fusarium etc . after much thought it occurred to me that it only started after i started to  fertilze  and it  also occurred at the end of the season after the feeds? . other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mindshift", "author_name": "mindshift", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mindshift", "date": "2021-12-20", "text": "I'm not going to recommend any particular plants. I don't know what type of soil you have or its pH. Your local nursery personnel know your local conditions and are better able to make recommendations. Right now you should search for internet articles on plants that fit your needs. You won't be able to plant until spring. Save articles and photos of things you like. Look for plants hardy to one zone colder than yours to make sure they make it through an unusually cold spell. You can clear out unwanted plants over winter. However, I'm leery of using a skid steer to clear a planting area around trees. The majority of any tree's roots are in the top 3' of soil. Damage to the roots is damage to the tree. English and similar ivies can be extremely persistent. They have deep roots and any bit left behind can resprout. Dig out what you can, but expect to have to come back and remove sprouts repeatedly to get rid of the plant. Some of your existing shrubs might be rejuvenated by cutting them back. General pruning either calls for all branches to be cut back by 1/3, or 1/3 of the oldest branches are cut back to ground level. Some shrubs can be cut back hard, but you need to look up each species for specific information. Shrubs are relatively low maintenance, and broadleaf and coniferous evergreens provide more winter interest than deciduous plants. Still, consider using shrubs with colorful or interesting winter stems, or fruit. The word \"dwarf\" only means smaller than the species, so pay attention to the expected mature size and spread listed on plants tags. Don't put a plant that will grow to 36\" wide closer than 18\" to a wall, fence or path. New shrubs will be small; the largest usually comes in a #3 pot. Don't place them too close together. It's best to fill in around them with annuals or low perennial ground covers. Don't over mulch. The main reason for mulch is to protect soil from rain. Large rain drops can hit the ground at 20 mph and splash soil particles up to 5' away. But mulch placed against the base of plants can lead to fungal disease. As plants grow they provide their own mulch in leaves. I think it best to apply a layer of compost around established plants than to continue to use mulch. A specimen shrub can stand on its own, but when adding colorful plants it is best to repeat them across the entire yard. Instead of pulling out all the boxwood across the front, perhaps you could just replace the two flanking the steps with a smaller shrub. That will visually expand your entry, and you can always replace the others later. I agree with getting rid of the shutters. None of your shutters look wide enough to actually cover the windows if they were operational. Those on the side are ridiculously small. Consider painting the window trim a contrasting color there.", "images": []}}

title: Musty/moldy smell from vents in home | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-346243456", "author_name": "Lindsey Hill", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-346243456", "date": "2021-12-20", "text": "Hello, Here's a real stumper for yall that, so far, no one can figure out. In early 2020, we had our HVAC unit replaced as well as all new ductwork. We live in Mooresville NC, a humid climate, and have a crawlspace. Our HVAC unit is a heat pump. A month or two after getting the new unit, we kept smelling strong musty smells from our vents. There was a 100+ sq foot section of the crawlspace, under a hall bathroom, full of mold. It was explained to us that the new hvac unit was strong enough now to pull in the smell whereas the old unit was not and therefore the mold was probably there for some time. We bought our house in October of 2018 and the seller did have a burst pipe fixed in that location. The south is notorious for crawlspace issues due to the intense humidity so none of this is a shock. Fast forward a few months-November 2020, and we have our crawlspace encapsulated, mold remediated, and a dehumidifier installed with the hopes that this would stop future growth should Another pipe burst, etc. Spring of 2021, we notice the smell come back when using the heat. We are told we need a \"soil odor fan\" as the smell may be coming from organismic growth between the soil and the vapor barrier. We sit on it over the summer because the AC does not smell and we're hopeful come winter 2021 we do not need it. Fast forward to October 2021, the heats on and it smells. Also, given we're in the south we do sometimes need AC in October and now the AC also smells. We try the soil odor fan and to no avail, more smell. So, it was uninstalled, and we were refunded. We discovered that the original mold is back, likely because it was not fully treated the first go-around...something was missed. The company comes back out, treats it, and it's gone. However, the smell is still present. My husband and I verified the mold is indeed gone and a moisture meter reads 10% everywhere in the crawlspace where wood is present. Now, six days ago, we have an HVAC air scrubber installed...this works for 4 days...and 2 days ago, the smell is back. All filters have been replaced multiple times, the HVAC unit has been cleaned, and the ductwork has been inspected thoroughly....no issues are noted with the HVAC system but the smell is only present when air is circulating. At this point, NO ONE knows what to do or who we should call for help.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "author_name": "Charles Ross Homes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "date": "2021-12-21", "text": "Hi, Lindsey, Most homes operate at slight negative pressure due to a combination of HVAC system issues and stack effect.   Duct work seams should be sealed with mastic designed for that purpose, but even meticulously installed HVAC ducts will leak.  A leaky return duct can indeed pull moisture, odors, and soil gases from the crawl space and the air handler will dutifully distribute them throughout the home.   Duct leakage can be tested (and quantified) with a duct blaster test. Most HVAC replacement work and most crawl space encapsulation work are performed without the benefit of permits or inspections.  And the majority of both are performed by individuals who don't know anything about basic building science principles, in my experience. It may not make sense at first, but a sealed, conditioned crawl space actually requires mechanical ventilation in order to comply with the building code. I'm betting your crawl space doesn't have any ventilation-- which would otherwise dilute the concentration of soil gases and odors-- or has a return opening from the crawl space which is the non-sensical of the two code-prescribed methods to ventilate a conditioned crawl space. The International Residential Code (IRC,) which forms the core of most statewide building codes, requires ventilation of \"unvented\" crawl spaces at a rate of 1 cfm/ 50 sq. ft. of floor area--which is not a lot.  The prescriptive methods to achieve that are listed in section R408.3 of the code.  Of the two prescribed methods, I recommend continuous mechanical exhaust.  I've found that the other prescribed method--supplying air from the HVAC supply can create localized conditions which favor growth of mold and mildew. Some of the earliest work evaluating methods to construct conditioned crawl spaces was performed by John Tooley in your home state of NC.    I believe he's retired now, but  he worked for Advanced Energy in Raleigh.  I suggest you give them a call.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "None of the above.  What you are seeing now are some winter annuals and not the summer annuals that the product would be expecting.  The time to spray herbicide is April 15th, tax day.  Mid April give the spring and summer weeds time to germinate and mature somewhat.  Actively growing weeds die better than dormant weeds.  The next time to use herbicide is September 15th.  Do that only if you have some spots that need it. Your best line of defense against weeds is proper watering.  Deep and infrequent is the mantra for watering.  Deep means 1 inch all at one time.  Frequency depends on the air temperatures.  With temps below 70 you should water deeply once a month unless you get rain.  With temps between 70 and 80 you should water once every 3 weeks.  With temps between 80 and 90 you should water deeply once every 2 weeks.  With temps in the 90s you should water once per week.  With temps above 100 you can water once every 5 days.  Where I live in Texas I can usually go 10 days to 2 weeks in the heat of summer (high 90s).  There are other factors like sun/shade, clouds, wind, soil type, grass type, humidity, and others I've forgot.  The main one is air temp, so go with that as your primary indicator.  Why do this?  Because weed seeds need continual moisture to germinate and take root.  If you are watering a little bit every day, that is perfect conditions for germinating weed seeds.  Of course Mother Nature often gets in the way of deep and infrequent watering plans, so you'll have to adjust.  If you get a week of rain in May, you're going to have a week problem in the summer.  Crabgrass loves a week of rain in May.", "images": []}}

Dakota Burgundy was planted 3 years ago.  They are long blooming, the bloom stalks and foliage are beautiful as well.  And when the snow melts, the foliage still looks fresh! 3- Nepeta: I have 4 varieties, my favorite one (by far) is Dropmore. They bloom for a long time and if you cut them back, you'll get more blooms, even with our short summers! 5- Tall phlox: they\u2019re beautiful and they smell great! :) 6- Achillea: I love these.  I\u2019ve had Terracotta for a few years and I added 2 more varieties in 2021.  They were still blooming at the end of September. 7- Veronicas: I planted White Wands 3 years ago and love it. And here\u2019s my list of top plants for striking blooms that reliably come back: 1- Darwin tulips: if you\u2019re in a deer-free area, you gotta try these.  I planted the first ones 7-8 years ago, and they\u2019ve always come back.  I read that they must be planted deeply, which I did.  Nothing beats tulips after a long winter. 2- Peonies: itohs and herbaceous.  They are new to my garden, except for Bowl of Beauty, but one of Canada's largest grower is very close to where I live, they grow both itohs and herbaceous so you'll be ok. 3- Iris: Bearded and Siberian.  My favorite Siberian is Pink Parfait, it has a longer bloom period than my other siberian.  It's too hard to pick a favorite tall bearded, but Don't Stop Believing was a show-stopper. 4- Clematis: I can never get them to look as good as what other people post online (mine look sparse in comparison), but still, the blooms are amazing. title: I need to cut a hole in the floor but there's a pipe in the way | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "gabis-daddi", "author_name": "Gabis Daddi", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gabis-daddi", "date": "2021-12-21", "text": "So I've got a new problem to deal with. My dishwasher broke, two years ago, and I just finally got the replacement. Because of the placement of the water feed on the floor the new unit simply will not fit. The pump is directly in line with the ball valve. The plumber already had taken off the handle to remove the unit and the two of us tried for over an hour to finagle the new one over the valve and it just cannot. The feed must be moved to the back which means cutting the floor. That brings me to you folks. I've got a rotozip, a dremel with many attachments and bits, and an oscillating saw. The floor there is probably 3/4 inch but my main concern is hitting that pipe because we have no idea which way it goes, or what's under the wood. There is no room underneath. The kitchen is cantilevered off the house so the only thing beneath it, that's visible, is soffit or siding or whatever you call it when it's on the ceiling and outside. Any thoughts on how to safely cut into the floor? Best case scenario is to cut out a large square in that space and reuse that wood. I'm not even sure if I can get 3/4 ply in my area, and I would only need a 2'x2' which even then would need need to be cut down.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5e42cdbc01c22ac5_0958-w500-h392-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gabis-daddi", "author_name": "Gabis Daddi", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gabis-daddi", "date": "2022-02-01", "text": "Today my dishwasher was installed so I thought I'd post a follow up. I did eventually get the floor piece up. It happened to be a 1/4 inch piece of lauan that was on the 3/4\" plywood subfloor. However, just that small square was stapled down with twenty two 1/4\" wide, one and a half inch long staples. Once the lauan was up I made a three inch hole in the center of the plywood and probed around, then cut out the plywood. There was actually a plywood seam there, so it was two pieces of plywood to be removed. The copper stub in the front middle was dead, as in there was nothing on the other end and it moved freely so it was removed. The big ball valve was removed, a 90 was added to move the line to the back and a very small valve was installed there. The pipe going to the back is resting on the joist. Then the removed plywood was recycled and put back on the joists (albeit in different orientations) and next to the new pipe. Lastly, the ugly lauan was put back over the plywood (it never even occurred to me to get a new piece until I looked at the pic that I added below). Then five minutes of cleanup, and twenty minutes later the new dishwasher had been installed and was running. The entire process took less than two hours.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/aa028b9201f8874f_7519-w240-h196-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/67a2a93f01f88750_7520-w240-h188-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

Pitched baffles seen in some residential hoods, such as Wolf Pro hoods, are an intermediate case that is closer to the horizontal configuration than the high commercial configuration. Generally, a hood width of 6 inches beyond the range width is considered adequate for residential cooking.  More refinement can be made from plume types and their divergence angles from the locus of potential pan areas, but for this message these details will be left unstated.  So we get 48 + 6 inches as a desired width. Front to back depth should be a deep as available from residential units, although one can get custom/bespoke designs of almost any configuration.  Assume that the hood aperture is 24 inches within a 27-inch hood (see Wolf Pro hood details).  This hood, then, has an entry aperture area of 4.5 x 2 = 9 square feet and should be adequate up to 36 inches above the pans.  (Note that I am working with a wall hood here and not an insert into a cabinet like structure.  What is available for such applications may not meet what is desirable in hood entry aperture sizing.) We need the airflow to be sufficient to deal with entraining the plumes into the baffle flow.  Worst case, this could be calculated from potential plume sizes and velocities, but given that residential hoods with low reservoir volumes cannot average plumes across the entire baffle space, some approximations are needed to achieve adequacy.  The one I like that is derived, in a sense, from the Greenheck method (https://www.tagengineering.ca/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/KVSApplDesign_catalog.pdf) is to assume that the baffle gap area is half the aperture area, and that the effective plume velocity can be 3 ft/s (peaks to 1.2 m/s have been observed).  This leads to a need for 180 ft/min in the baffle gaps, or 90 ft/min across the aperture.  No one here building to that standard has yet complained about inadequate flow, so we will go with 90 ft/min. 90 ft/min x 9 sq. ft. is 810 CFM.  That is the desired actual flow rate at full blower power.  Blowers are rated for free air (zero static pressure) performance, and this will need to be about 1.5 times the requirement to make up for (at a minimum) baffle pressure loss. Best quieting with standard residential components is a roof blower with a large enough duct and an intermediate silencer. Commercial applications require grease capture at the blower, in addition to at the baffles. title: Air quality: burning lungs, nervousness/depression, gas leaks | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-739022174", "author_name": "HU-739022174", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-739022174", "date": "2021-12-22", "text": "Hi. I\u2019m writing this message for people searching the internet who may have faced the same issue I\u2019ve been trying to resolve the last year, and finally have. I will just say, my house made me extremely sick. Tingling lips, hot/cold eyes, upper respiratory/chest pain, nervousness/depression in home. We were directed to a million different ideas to direct; mold, radon, ect.. but after working with an air quality specialist the last year he let me know my symptoms aligned with a gas leak. So we contacted local plumbing to bring their gas sniffer out and test all our gas fired appliances gas lines and fittings. Turns out we were living with two major gas leaks; one in furnace one in hot water heater. Got those corrected, still was having overall chest pain/nervousness. Our second major issue was our furnace was going bad. We had two different HVAC companies come out to test furnace with a combustion analyzer tool which measures carbon monoxide. The first hvac company only tested vents indoors and came up with \u201c3\u201d reading meaning very little to no carbon monoxide levels in home. Contacted a second HVAC opinion, they tested indoors (same result) and outdoors at HVAC exhaust reading levels of \u201c145\u201d (anything below 50 at exhaust is normal) we could also smell the exhaust as walking up to it.. so pay attention if your exhaust emitting odors. Anyways, that HVAC was in no rush to put in new furnace due to stating \u201cheat exchanger going bad, but it\u2019s exhausting outside and not inside according to combustion analyzer\u201d I contacted air quality and they stated that even tho furnace is not picking up carbon monoxide indoors it most likely is setting off a flue gas that the monitor wouldn\u2019t pick up. Long story short after correcting gas leaks and new furnace I can finally live in our home again after a year of complete hell trying to figure out these problems. Only writing this in hopes of helping someone in the future. That is all.", "images": []}

All patent rights are country specific. If there is no granted patent in the US the innovator cannot enforce some other country's patent here. Pending patent (applications) are not enforceable until they are granted at which point limited damages may be claimed for the period when the application was pending and infringement occurred. As a home gardener I would generally only worry about granted US patents. The best place to look for them is here using key words: US Patent Full-Text Database Boolean Search (uspto.gov) If you have a specific query I would be happy to help. Trademarks are also country specific although it is a bit more complicated. There are commonlaw trademark rights that accrue from use even if they are not formally registered. title: Bought a lot of fixtures myself--did I make the showroom people mad? | Houzz Forum

We like our builder. We told him we were going to pick out and purchase our own lights and appliances, and some of the plumbing, and he was fine with that. We've got it all in storage, checked to see if it was in good shape on delivery, and are ready to take down the road to the building site when ready. If I forgot a doohickey, I can run to the hardware store and get it (i.e. a plug or connector). In particular, we LOVE our non-modern farmhouse funky lights. They are very much \"us.\" I got some excellent deals with coupons, and most things are known brands (Moen, Kraus, Delta, Shades of Light, Harbor Breeze, Bosch appliances). I'd like to see something solid /near-solid to break up what will end up being an awful lot of same-same-same.  To go with these tiles, gray makes sense.  Where to put it?  Maybe on the countertops?  Not the floor; the floor is much too large to go with a gray ... not in a room without natural light.  Gray on the shower floor would look good. Now some thoughts on the layout: - Look at your door swings:  You want to reverse your bathroom entry door so you enter and are \"oriented towards\" the room /not running into a wall /walking around the door to enter.  Similarly, you probably want the linen closet door to open towards the main room. - Are those 33\" bathroom sinks?   A 33\" sink in the kitchen is a great idea, but why in the world would you want something that large for the bathroom?  And why would you ever want a duplicate of that large sink?  Look at a yardstick and ask yourself whether this is really where you want to splurge. - Next to those massive sinks, you have 15\" drawers.  Note that the sides /hardware will eat up 3-4\", so you'll have 11-12\" actual drawer space at the sink.  This isn't bad storage, but it's also not exactly generous, especially given the size of this bathroom ... I'd cut those sinks down /go with a standard 18-22\" sink and allow yourself more at-sink storage. - You have roughly 8'x8' empty space in the middle of this room.  Why?  You could literally put a king-sized bed in this bathroom.  This is a lot to tile, and it serves no purpose.  Unless you're planning to bring in a bathroom seating area or exercise equipment or MMA fights, this large empty space will feel cold, especially since you don't have a window in this bathroom.  Think again about how this large empty space with all your working-parts floating around the edge will look in reality. - Yet with all this empty space, your shower is modest in size.  I had a shower that exact size in my old house, and while it was perfectly serviceable, it was not luxurious.  I can't see going with a modest shower and all that empty space. - Your shower head should be on the other end of the shower enclosure ... but keep your controls by the door (so you can turn on the shower without walking in).  With the shower head on the left side, you'll be able to step into the shower without being directly in the water stream.  Having your shower head \"back up to\" a closet is a wise choice ... it means that a plumber could access your shower's internal workings by cutting through your closet drywall /not your expensive shower tile.  I have an access panel in my linen closet that allows access to plumbing.  Because plumbing will one day break, that's future-proofing. - Where will you hang your shower towels? - I always dislike toilets-in-closets, especially since this one is stealing the only window in the whole large bathroom.  And yours is minimal in size.  36\" wide feels narrow, even to a small person like me.  It's like using a bathroom stall in a store, and you have no storage by the toilet ... no space for extra toilet paper or medical needs you may develop as you age.  Even if you want a toilet-in-a-closet, why would you make it minimal in size, while you have all this empty space in the middle of the room? - If you lose the linen closet, you could enlarge the shower ... it's also going to cause an odd viewpoint as you enter the room. main_question: {"author_id": "jason-carlton26", "author_name": "Jason, zone 7A, near Greensboro NC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jason-carlton26", "date": "2021-12-23", "text": "My girlfriend and I are at an impasse :-O  So I need design help! There's a weird half wall in the middle, though, and stairs on the other side, so the actual usable space for the living room is about 12' x 12'. For whatever reason, that level stays MUCH colder than the upstairs (offices, bathrooms, and bedroom). So she wants to put in an electric fireplace for additional heat. I'm OK with the idea, and think it should be in the (unused) dining room against an exterior wall. I could easily cut the baseboard and chair rail to make it look like it belongs there, then mount a mirror on top of it to add depth to the room. But she hates that idea, and is afraid that the heat won't go around the weird half wall to heat up the living room area. She would rather replace the TV stand with a console that has a built-in fireplace. The TV is 47\", and is against that weird half wall (not an exterior wall). Due to the weird layout of the floor, that's really the only place that the TV CAN be. To me, this has a few flaws: 1. Being against an interior wall doesn't look like it's a natural part of the house, since there obviously couldn't be a chimney there; 2. We would have to have the console a little off of the wall to make room for wires, and since you would see it from the side when you walk in to the room it doubles-down on the obviousness of it not being real; 3. The ones we're finding are 30+ tall, and if we put the TV on top of that then we'll have to look upwards to watch it instead of straight-on like we do now. And another issue for me... I have yet to see a console / fireplace that didn't look cheap and ugly :-/  We're getting dangerously close to 50 years old, I don't want to have furniture that looks like the quality I had when I was 19! What were your favorite books this year? Here\u2019s my list (in no particular order): Anxious People \u2013 Fredrik Backman. I\u2019ve loved all his books and this one, filled with quirky characters and an inept kidnapper/robber, was thoroughly original and enjoyable. Piranesi \u2013 Susanna Clarke. This book was like nothing I had ever read before. It took a while to figure out and nothing about it was straightforward, but the journey was fascinating and I was amazed by her imagination. The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue \u2013 V.E. Schwab. A modern fairy tale about a young girl who wishes for the wrong thing to escape an arranged marriage. This thought experiment \u2013 what if you could live forever, but nobody remembered you? \u2013 was terrific. Have You Seen Luis Velez? \u2013 Catherine Ryan Hyde. This was a feel-good choice for my book group, an uplifting story of a young man doing the right thing. In a difficult year this was balm for the soul. The whole book group loved it. The Rose Code \u2013 Kate Quinn. I wound up reading this book twice, it was that good. The best thing I\u2019ve read this year, bar none. The Huntress was also excellent. The Murderbot Diaries \u2013 Martha Wells. Recommended here, and I\u2019m so very grateful to have read them! This sci-fi series about a robot/human construct who overrides its programming and then must deal with the humans around it in order to survive was brilliant. Project Hail Mary \u2013 Andy Weir. Just as good as The Martian, this tale of desperate attempt to save Earth and a very reluctant hero was fabulous. There\u2019s a movie in the works, as there should be, LOL. Spinning Silver & Uprooted \u2013 Naomi Novak. These two fairytale-style fantasy stories featured strong female characters and I was completely engrossed in both of them.  I'd never read anything by her before and thought both were wonderfully done. Nightbitch \u2013 Rachel Yoder. Another book unlike any other I\u2019ve read, this story of a stay-at-home-mother\u2019s unraveling as she begins to believe she\u2019s a dog is underpinned by her ferocious love for her toddler son. Definitely not for everybody, and difficult to read in spots, it had lots of important (IMHO) things to say about women, marriage, motherhood, and society. Hamnet \u2013 Maggie O\u2019Farrell. title: Benefits of Bespoke Fitted Furniture over Shop bought | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "2d-carpentry-pfvwgb-pf~1329833748", "author_name": "2D Carpentry", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/cabinets-and-cabinetry/2d-carpentry-pfvwgb-pf~1329833748", "date": "2021-12-24", "text": "Having fitted furniture in your home is an excellent way of making use of spaces that are otherwise unusable or unable to use to its full potential.It\u2019s an investment that you benefit from everyday and even makes your home more desirable to potential buyers. Bespoke furniture gives you the freedom to choose exactly the layout you want to make the most of the space and enable you to make better use of the area with no wasted space beside the units. title: Need Advice on Keiki | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "dsegel", "author_name": "dsegel", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dsegel", "date": "2021-12-25", "text": "I have a well established phalaenopsis that has bloomed at least 3 times.  It lives in SW FL in the shade of our lanai.  Recently it developed a keiki which now has two small leaves and one very long root (bottom right on picture).  Today I noticed the mother plant is also growing a flower stalk (to the left of the keiki in the pic).  I hate to do it, but should I cut off the flower shoot until the keiki is big enough to be cut off?  Or is the keiki ready to be severed from the mother (I've read it should have multiple leaves and at least 2 or 3 roots)  ?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4cc2b5ce01c676ee_2021-w500-h236-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-353955525", "author_name": "Billsc", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-353955525", "date": "2021-12-25", "text": "Desgel,  I found a few spare minutes, so let me say thank you for the good pictures.  They show exactly what I was asking to see.  Now, lets make you a happy camper.  I agree completely with getgoing, it appears you have a healthy, happy, reproducing Phalaenopsis.  I, also recommend you leave that little  keiki where it is at least until it has two leaves as large as the one that's on it now.   That's going to create an interesting potting challenge for you, because you seem to have one of those plants that loves to produce difficult to repot roots.   You might want to consider some cotton string and another stake or two, to gently, over the next few months, try convincing that root to grow off in a direction more compatible with potting.  Right now, if you plant the root down in the pot, the crown of the plant will be facing the side of the pot. title: Are my soapstone countertop expectations unreasonable? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-741289418", "author_name": "M M", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-741289418", "date": "2021-12-25", "text": "We elected soapstone for our current kitchen remodel. I understand that soapstone is on the softer side, ages/patinas, and will show wear and usage much more than a harder material. I'm fine with this (in fact, prefer it) and I do not expect perfection in the material- neither over the long haul or during fabrication/installation. Unfortunately, there was an issue during the fabrication. We were not informed of this by the fabricator- I had to spot the issue myself (which wasn't hard as you will see). I've spoken to the fabricator who says he aims to make it right. Evidently, when the corners were drilled for the sink opening the bit skipped (paraphrasing him here) and damaged the surface next to the sink. The original damage. It's the zig-zaggy mark on the surface, and accompanied by a fissure on the inside surface/edge of the sink. I found this a bit of a bummer, but I was on the fence as to whether or not I could live with this as-is. It was a pretty deep groove. Not sure if you can see that in the photo adequately.   There was a somewhat unfortunate attempt to remedy this (without my knowledge as the installer returned to fix an unsightly unevenness in the reveal which was off by about 1/4-3.8\"). My estimation is that the patchwork now looks even worse and I'm almost certainly unable to live with it how it looks now. The following two photos show the attempt to fix it. It is now very, very obvious.     So, that's a bummer- but not the actual topic of my question about expectations. I had previously not inspected the countertops closely, but since this series of events I took a closer look. There are no fewer than 20 other (albeit minor) scratches on the countertops. Now... The countertops are otherwise beautiful and do contain lots of natural details. Some of those details look like natural fissures, cracking, scratching, etc. as you would expect on a soapstone countertop. The countertops, though, are (aside from the scratches I'm pointing out) smooth as a baby's bottom. I mention this because I want to be clear that the scratches in these photos do not look (and are not) naturally occurring and are also not at all smooth. That is, you can run a fingernail over then and feel the snag of the crack. I'm including just a couple of pics to give you a flavor, including a chip in the rounded part, and something that appears to have been affixed to the countertop with adhesive (likely during the installation). There are seriously 20 post-its on my countertop with scratches like the following pics.           I assume that these defects can be remedied (sanding/oiling). However, I Was on the fence about oiling the countertops. I kinda didn't want to, but it seems that I might have to to help mask any sanding fixes for these defects. I probably wouldn't have worried about these additional scratches if not for the poor initial installation and the damage that occurred during fabrication that I had to find and inquire about myself. But that got me to looking more closely and now I'm bothered by them. My expectations were basically pretty minimal (in my opinion): don't damage the countertops during fabrication nor installation, and don't deliver them with 20+ scratches. My question is this. With respect to the scratches other than the big one- am I being unreasonable in my expectations?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0b42840b01c748a8_0217-w500-h436-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d0a2905c01c748a9_0218-w500-h424-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/8ea2ae8d01c748aa_0219-w500-h474-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2722886c01c748ac_0221-w500-h486-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ec92847b01c748ad_0221-w500-h526-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/04e298df01c748ae_0223-w500-h659-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1e7281e801c748af_0223-w500-h484-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1632af5b01c748b0_0224-w500-h527-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "julieste", "author_name": "julieste", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/julieste", "date": "2021-12-26", "text": "I'm just another homeowner who has soapstone counters (for eight years in my primary home and just installed in a secondary home). Here is my take. The big mark by the sink edge definitely needs to be remedied. I am also speaking as someone who just had to ask my fabricator to re-do two different major, major issues (screw-ups) on my recent install; he complied even though I suspect doing so cost him his profit on my job. As far as all of the little scratches, that's part and parcel of soapstone. Once you are at the point where you aren't so hyper focused on trying to find flaws in the counters, you will happily live with and accept your counters. Sometimes I think that participating in this forum pushes many of us into the hyper critical mode. I know often in the past I've gone back and taken a long, hard look at my kitchen and see that I have issues--water spotting or minor white dents in my marble counters, for example--that I had never even though about  until I read here about people fretting about them. title: Your most memorable Christmas | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "marilyn-c", "author_name": "marilyn_c", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/marilyn-c", "date": "2021-12-26", "text": "I meant to start this a day or so ago, but I guess better late than never. As I have mentioned before, after my dad died in 1968, the family more or less drifted apart.   We used to all meet at our parents' house, but after dad died, my  mother started going to my brother's.   My sister didn't get along with him, so she didn't go.   My niece and nephew that I had grown up with, were gone...my nephew to the Navy, and my niece went to West Texas to be a nanny.   I later found out she was pregnant, and that was why my sister sent her, but I didn't learn of this until many years later. This was in 1970: We had company...a guy that we went to high school with, who had fallen on hard times, and he (and his horse) were staying with us for awhile.   Jody was just getting over pneumonia.   I fixed turkey and all the trimmings, and afterwards Jody asked me if I would like to go for a drive...any where I wanted to go.   The friend was taking a nap on the couch, but he would be available to feed horses if we got back late. I had recently read an article in the Houston newspaper about a big pet cemetery, where everything from a hamster to a horse was buried.  It was on the far side of Houston...but that is where I wanted to go.   (Yes, I have always been weird). I don't know how we ever found the place...this before gps or Google maps.   I imagine we probably had a regular fold out, paper, map.   We found it.   I recall it was kind of out in the country off of Campbell Road. It was already late in the afternoon.   There was a chapel near the front.   We walked around looking at graves and reading the headstones.   Sentiments like, \"Born a dog, Died our baby\".   Near the front was a grave with a Christmas tree on it.   It had that white, sparkly material, like people sometimes put around Christmas trees, covering the little grave, and dog toys laid upon it. It was getting dark...the sun had gone down.   We were getting ready to leave, when a stationwagon pulled up.   An old couple got out, with a little chihuahua dog on a leash.   The man walked over to the chapel, which obviously had an outside electrical plug, and plugged in lights that lit up the Christmas tree on the little grave.   The old lady rearranged the dog toys. We were standing off in the distance, but I started crying...tears running down my face.   Jody said, \"What's the matter...why are you crying?\" I said \"It is just so sad.   Obviously they have no one, and are alone.\" Jody said, \"Aw, stop crying...look at us.   We drove all the way over here on Christmas day...\" I did get the point.   Still, it was sad, and we left without being intrusive to them.   I can still see it...clear as a bell, to this day. That area is very built up now.  I looked for Houston Pet Cemetery on google but didn't find it.   Probably a high rise office building on it now.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "shannon-wi", "author_name": "Shannon_WI", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/shannon-wi", "date": "2021-12-26", "text": "Ideally, the hood should be 6\u201d wider than the cooktop, so in your case, 42\u201d wide. (B) the size of the duct that goes from the hood to the outside.  It needs to have an 8\u201d or 10\u201d diameter depending on the hood.
