title: Juniper wintering question-need quick advice!! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mindazetlin", "author_name": "mindazetlin", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mindazetlin", "date": "2021-12-27", "text": "I have a juniper semi-cascade (I think) bonsai that I've had for about 25 years. Needless to say, I'm quite attached to this tree! When I lived in the Northeastern US, where winters can be quite cold, I would bury it up to the trunk in the compost pile right before the temperature sank into the 20s every year. Snow would cover it also and it would be fine when I pulled it out in spring. A few years ago, we moved to Snohomish, near Seattle. Winter temperatures here are often above freezing and only rarely do they go down to the mid-20s that would be bad for the tree. So for the years we've been living here (except for once, when I went traveling through February) I've simply left it outdoors and on the rare night when sub-25 temperatures were expected, just brought it in and set it by the window for that one night. But now we're having a cold snap that's going to last a week. I brought the tree in last night as per usual, not realizing how long the cold was going to last. Now I have a dilemma. 1) If I leave it indoors by the window at night for the whole week, will that mess with its dormancy? I'm afraid it could. I could put it outside during the day only some days--it's going to be quite cold--but then I'd have to bring it in at night so it would be experiencing temperature changes daily. 2) I can still bury it in the compost pile as the ground has not yet frozen. I'm thinking maybe that's what I should do. But now it will have spent 48 hours indoors, so I'm concerned about shocking it. Maybe do it during the warmest part of the day tomorrow? And then, once it's in the compost, should I leave it there till spring? (Which comes very early here anyhow.) I would be heartbroken if anything bad happened to this tree. Any quick advice will be appreciated.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2021-12-28", "text": "What species of juniper is it? They're not all created equal insofar as their ability to tolerate low temperatures. If it's J chinensis/ Shimpaku or J procumbens, J rigida, J horizontalis, leave it outdoors during cold snaps. If temps are to be below 25*, make sure it's resting directly on the ground or on the floor of an unheated garage where rising geothermal heat will help keep its feet warmer than ambient air temps. Leaving it on the ground and covering it temporarily with a box or tub is also an option. If you have some dry leaves, it would be good to provide mulch enough to cover the pot all the way to the lowest foliage. You needn't worry about the foliage, only the roots. You could also situate it on the ground or in a window well on the north side of a heated building and mulch the pot. I left several J procumbens and J chinensis \"Shimpaku\" on the grow benches through last year's winter and all awoke with no discernible reason to think they were worse for the exposure, even though they suffered through almost 2 weeks of temps in double digits below ) at night and single digit daily highs. These were just free plants in nursery cans given to me by a friend who owns a nursery and I had no time invested in them.  I'm not recommending that type of treatment as a habit as I understand that root damage from chill occurs incrementally. IOW, the finest roots are first to succumb and as temps continue to fall, thicker roots also fall victim to the chill. I can't be more specific about killing lows because it varies so much by species. Al", "images": []}}

If you have a 10\" deep pot, when the top 2\" of the grow medium feels dry to the touch, the bottom 6\" of the soil column could easily be 100% saturated. The commonly offered advice to water when the top inch or two of the soil feels dry is fine if the pot is 5\" deep or less, but serves as little more than a recipe for over-watering in deeper pots. What's important is what moisture levels are at the bottom of the pot. To monitor for moisture deep in the pot, I suggest you use a homemade \"tell\" made from a wood dowel rod (any hardware or big box store like Lowes, Home Depot, Menards. If you water your plant when the dowel comes out only slightly moist, you'll avoid stress associated with both over and under-watering. Water meters, the inexpensive ones, don't measure moisture levels. They measure electrical conductivity, and as such they are notoriously unreliable. Using a \"tell\" would serve you much better. Plants make and store their own energy source \u2013 photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water \u2013 so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16\u201d (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48\u201d (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. title: Crawlspace Water Advice Needed for new build | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-523083381", "author_name": "Lora P", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-523083381", "date": "2021-12-27", "text": "Hi Houzz!  I have been really impressed with the cumulative advice out there and I was wondering if anyone could weigh in on what might be a unique crawlspace water problem we are having in our new build in a unique location. Okay - so we are building a home in an old reservoir.   It's overwhelming and crazy but everyone said it would be fine.   It is an amazing site.   Here is the backstory - A natural rock bowl on the side of a hill was dammed up 150 years ago and for a period of about 30 years, it supplied our city with water until the city outgrew it.  It does not have a natural water source; water was pumped in from a river that is downhill of it - like 1/2 mile away.  The dam now has a firetruck approved arch through it put in by the previous owners so water readily flows out through it and the open pipe that flows out under the dam (think tub drain that there is no plug for) - there is never accumulation of water in the dam.  Because this lot was undeveloped for many years and was city owned, the houses around it that were built in the 1960's and 70's designed their lots to drain into ours.  California has been in a drought for a few years so no one else really appreciated the amount of water that would flow through the lot until we have been having heavy rains the past couple of months. So, fast forward to now.  We developed the property, ran utilities to the center of the bowl, and have built our house there with a garage slab foundation and the rest of the house over a crawlspace.  There was a natural flow of water that ran down the middle of the property and we designed the house to miss this flow and be on a higher part of the bowl, but when the foundation layout was staked, we realized the design engineering firm had made a mistake in their topo and the side of the house was in the middle of a giant rock outcropping, so we had to shift the house over 8 feet such that the corner now eclipses the place the water previously naturally flowed. There is a design for drainage that the architect made that has not been fully executed.  Swales aren't in place and it's not graded correctly yet. But, at this point, we aren't sure if the design is sufficient given the amount of water in the crawlspace (mostly under the vapor barrier, but some gets on top with the joints not appropriately sealed).  The construction engineering firm designed additional drainage quoted at $30,000 including french drains around 50% of the house (there is a lot of rock and they plan to go 3 ft down).  We aren't sure if A. This will work or B. Is necessary with the amount of rock around the house.  I am thinking we might bring in a crawlspace company now to give us their thoughts and a quote and/or landscapers, but my spouse wants to wait and try to carry out the architect's plan plus a few surface drains and then bring in the crawl space experts  and landscapers when we are done with the house (we are 2-3 months away from completion) and the site is not under a GC's control.  My thought is that crawl space experts will have seen problems like this before and might be better at figuring out the right solution the first time. Foundation is dug down to bedrock, quickrete, then stem walls.  Crawl space is 3 to 6 feet tall. So, any thoughts at this point with info provided?  Should we bring in a crawl space expert now?  Will they be able to advise on drainage?  Advice re area drains versus French drains in a highly rocky area (that's why they put a reservoir here)?  How bad is it to have some water flowing under the vapor barrier (there is a drain that it gets out of so it is mostly not sitting water)?", "images": []}

Plus we dog sit a lot and have experience with a lot of breeds (e.g. Airedales, border collies, Lab and Lab x Australian Shepherd, Australian terrier, Springer Spaniel, malamute, Bouvier, Briard, Boston terrier, and others....)  It's important to pay attention to the dog's needs and wants and accommodate those in the garden!  All dogs want to patrol their territory, so a path that largely follows the boundary of the space is desirable - otherwise they will make their own!   Most dogs will literally 'take the path of least resistance' so having planned paths through beds helps keep them from wandering through the plantings at random :-)  Before we laid out most of the paths, we watched the dogs to see what their normal route was and, as much as possible, put the paths there :-)  Kids also tend to like and follow paths through the garden beds :-)  So, watch where your dog goes and see what that tells you about what it needs in the garden :-)   If there are wet places in the garden, they need fixing - add drainage or redirect the waterflow or plant appropriate plants that will make use of the water and ideally provide support with their roots.  We have several places like that here, most of which have been improved over time by various means.  The picture below is from 2014 when the paths in 'the wet corner' area were in bad shape so DH and a nephew added 'crusher run' gravel that was then covered in pine bark mulch to make it disappear!  The low iron fence at the edge in the picture was there to keep the Golden we had back in the early years here out of this area after she, in the first year here, regularly came back covered in mud!  She could have easily stepped over the fence but it was sufficient to tell her that this was a no-go area!  One important thing we did here was shape the spaces - particularly the little grass that remains! - so that it makes the space have impact regardless of the season.  If that space is kept reasonably neat, the whole garden looks organized even if it is a bit messy (e.g. needs some weeding or pruning etc.!)  You could consider the shape of your grass spaces plus the paths.  Some people consider it a formal look but it works well with informal plantings! other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "vivid-blue", "author_name": "Vivid Blue", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/vivid-blue", "date": "2022-02-05", "text": "Our leathered granite is Via Lactea, very different from yours (black with white veining) but it did the same thing when it was first installed.  I actually think for ours that it was because the granite is so dense (ie. non-porous), so the \"sealer\" just sat on top and the streaks were actually in the sealer. After a few weeks of cleaning with soap and hot water, the streaks went away and we have had no problems since then.  It's been five years and it's pretty impervious to everything (olive oil, red wine, etc.). If you can, Google the name of your granite and see if you can find a spec sheet.  The absorbency (\"Water absorption\" or maybe \"Absorption by weight\") on our granite is 0.14% which is really low. So if your granite has a similarly low number then perhaps it doesn't need sealer. :) Best of luck!", "images": []}}

We've hired a contractor and signed a contract, etc. I've obsessed and dreamt of this kitchen for years and I don't plan on moving until the funeral home carts me out. I want it to be as historically sensitive as possible spanning 1900 to 1920s. I've got a 1920s Hotpoint stove, a monitor top refrigerator, and an antique display cabinet (about 7 feet by 11 feet)  that I'm including in the design. While I would LOVE some Kennebec or Crown Point cabinetry, I'm a public school teacher and my husband a steelworker - so you can imagine we don't have a ton to spend on this. I believe in the contract we were allotted 12,000 for cabinets. It's not a huge number of cabinets (to me) - Pantry/2 corner bases/ sink base/ 12 and 24-inch bases/double oven surround (and maybe 2 upper cabinets) - Here is my dilemma. Based on historical pictures and standing homes, I think the cabinets should be inset door. My contractor doesn't work with any companies that do inset doors, so he has me looking at Cliq Studios. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "Beyond VaH repelling me with their \"Magic Lung\" claims,* duly parroted by the sales force, I came to realize that the best residential hood (defined as one that fits below an 8-foot ceiling) is one that is least deviant from commercial hood practices.  This includes having baffle filters. Wolf answers their phone.  Their telephone contact connected me with one of their engineers who provided me with fan curves for several of their blowers, which are (were) manufactured by NuTone.  Fan curves are essential for performance estimation, and at the time (2007) pretty rare except in the aerospace industry. As to relative performance of VaH hoods in the noise category, I think @clinresga provided measured data in a thread here back around 2010.  There may be differences with modern VaH hoods. Others here have commented on cleaning difficulty; some recent comments suggest that this may have been somewhat improved in the past decade. VaH have also leaked some fan curve data.  What these show is that their squirrel cage blowers appear to be more sensitive than radial centrifugal blowers in flow vs. pressure loss.  VaH may now make more conventional hoods, I have no need to investigate them unless a specific question arises. In any case, I wanted an outside (roof) blower.  This moves a source of noise away from the hood and allows a Fantech silencer to occupy some of the duct length.  Blower noise is significantly reduced.  Remote blower operation can also allow in-line axial blowers, where they might have merit, and optionally roof-mounted commercial up-blast blowers that can be sized to run very quietly if oversized for the purpose. ---- *VaH like to claim that their x CFM blower(s) is/are equivalent to 1.5x standard blowers (that might fit in the same hood).  All they are really saying is that because they don't use baffles for grease extraction, they save on that pressure loss.  But there are other pressure losses that affect overall flow rate.  These include duct length, duct transitions, vent caps, and most significantly, how well the MUA brings the kitchen pressure close to the outside pressure.  So the achieved flow depends on the fan curve and the resistance curve of the entire hood and MUA systems. Note that blower rated CFM is a free air (zero static pressure) value and bears little resemblance to the actual CFM obtained in a system.  VaH CFM is (I hope) that of the blower(s) and hood combined, but not counting any other factor.", "images": []}}

title: Central Vacuum Advice Wanted! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-794657087", "author_name": "Sienna", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-794657087", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "I would like to get some information on central vacuums from the Houzz community. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-29576370115", "author_name": "M H", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-29576370115", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "I grew up with a central vacuum system and had one installed in my current home when it was built 9 years ago.  I'm not an expert but did a lot of research over the years so here's my take on your questions. 1) Best Brands - My parents built a big, brick house (Home Alone house) back in the late 80's and their builder put in a Nutone unit as many other homes in the neighborhood had.  It worked fine but sometime around 2000 the motor unit burned out and my parents replaced it with a MD Silentmaster unit.  Both are bagged units but only needed to be emptied a few times each year.  In my current home, our builder put in a Vacuflo copycat filtered cyclonic unit with the Dirt Devil label.   It was very powerful and very loud.  Emptying the bagless canister was disgusting and dog hair and dust would coat the pleated filter so with each emptying you had to remove the filter and bang it against the ground.  There would just be a giant dust cloud.  I'm not sad that the motor died within three years. We replaced it with a bagged MD central vac unit like my parents.  It's much quieter, very powerful and so easy to change the bags when needed.  I will never go back to a bagless central vac system. 2) Installation Considerations - Both my parents and myself had our builders put the system in so we didn't provide too much input.  I did get to pick the general location of the inlets but not the exact placement. There are a couple of inlets I would have preferred to be in a different spot based on furniture placement. For instance, the one in our family room is on the wall behind our couch.  Granted, our couch floats in the big room so it's not blocked but just would prefer it be on a different wall.  We have regular inlets for use with an electric hose as well as vacpans to sweep up small messes without needing the hose.  About a year or two into owning this house I had an installer put in a \"Hide a Hose\" inlet on the main level of our home.  If I were building again, I would only install the Hide a Hose inlets.  I am not a fan of dragging around the long hose and wrapping it up when I'm done as you do with a traditional system.  They now make battery-powered electric heads for hide a hose which work just as well as a normal powerhead.  We also made sure to have an inlet in the garage so that we can clean our cars and garage floors.  If I were to do it again, I'd have two.  One in the front of the garage by the driveway and one on the unit as it is now. 3) Maintenance & care - The bagged units are virtually maintenance free.  In the last six years I haven't done anything with the MD unit besides change the bag. Overall, I think I will always have a central vac in the homes I live in.  However, I don't think that they are for everyone.  If you're someone like me who uses the hose attachments a lot for dusting, cleaning dog hair off the couch, etc. then they're a great option.  But if you just want something to quickly do your floors then a regular vacuum might make more sense.  My parents are in their 70s and never really use their central vac anymore.  They no longer have kids or pets in the house so they get by with a Riccar upright and Dyson cordless.  I also have a Dyson cordless and self-emptying Roomba that get a lot of use.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-867564120", "author_name": "HU-867564120", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-867564120", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "We acted as the general contractor on our home build 15 years ago, so we installed a Beam central vac system. The power unit is in my basement workshop and the discharge is plumbed outside via its own dryer-style vent. Its a bagless unit and does a geat job. My big plus is that the discharge, which has to contain some sort of dust/dirt particles when using any vacuum, goes to the outside, its not recycled into the house. title: Miele Masterchef: Help in REDUCING programmed cooking time? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "janean-laidlaw", "author_name": "Janean Laidlaw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/janean-laidlaw", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "I finally (long story) replaced older 30\" Miele double ovens with the H6880 BP 30\" double ovens (after swearing that I would NEVER buy Miele again!). The top oven is plumbed for steam, and I have to admit that so far I am loving the \"Moistur Plus\" feature. I am a serious bread baker, and have been producing about 3-4 authentic(-ish) French baguettes every week, to the surprise and delight of family and friends -- including two really-French friends, who have been astonished at the authenticity of the baguettes' crusts. I have also experienced excellent results with rye bread (onion rye is very popular), plain old yeast rolls (which do not require steam), and Anadama bread, among other offerings. But the \"true\" French baguettes are the stars of the show. My only complaint is this:  I have found that for the baguettes (and for these only) I have to \"cheat\" the Masterchef program; I have to fight with the Masterchef pre-sets!  The crust \"darkness\" gauge/bar must always be on the LIGHTEST POSSIBLE setting, and even at that the resulting crust is still just barely-barely light enough. (Any browner a crust, and I would consider the result to be borderline burned.) And, here's the real catch:  I have to take the loaves out of the oven a full eleven minutes before the official end of the Masterchef program. I would be happy to come up with my own version of this \"Masterchef\" program, and set it as a \"Favorite,\" by using the manual steam fature and whatever combination[s] of cooking mode, temperature[s], and time will produce the same end result as does the Masterchef program. But so far, my own experiments haven't worked as well as does the simple expedient of using the Miele pre-programmed Masterchef \"baguette\" setting, minus eleven minutes of cooking time. The problem? While it is possible to ADD cooking time to a \"Masterchef\" program, I have searched and asked in vain to find a way to be able to SUBTRACT cooking time from an automatic, pre-fab \"Masterchef\" program. And it's a damned nuisance to hang around the kitchen to catch the program before it over-bakes the baguettes, every time. Does anyone know a work-around? A way to force a Masterchef pre-set program to REDUCE the programmed baking time? (Posting this as both a reply to a relevant thread and as a stand-alone question.) Any help would be most gratefully accepted!", "images": []}

title: How to determine if duct change is ok? Amateur load calculations... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "dave-johnson155", "author_name": "Dave Johnson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dave-johnson155", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "I recently had my central air replaced, as mentioned in this other post. The old main supply plenum had 3 separate 12\" ducts coming out of it to supply the downstairs. I noticed after the work was done that there are now only 2x 12\" junctions at the plenum, because 2 of those 12\" ducts were joined a few feet downstream from the plenum. See image below. The silver duct is new, joining an old black duct into another old black duct just downstream of the plenum and the damper.   I wonder if I should be concerned about this? Commence amateur load calculations. A 12\" duct has cross-sectional area 113 sq in. So... Now, it's worth pointing out that (a) it's a 5-ton system with a 20x36 filter intake and (b) the plenum itself is roughly 20\" square, so no more than 400 sq in could move through the system at a given time anyway, and the downstairs of the house is only like 1700 sq ft (compared to 1300 for the upstairs), so maybe 225 sq in is enough for the downstairs? But another way to view this is that maybe the two ducts that were joined now get a relatively smaller airflow compared to the 3rd duct which stayed alone? More amateur calculations incoming. There are  a total of 8 vents downstairs. I measured the metal duct diameter exiting into every vent. See chart below, explanation to follow:   The sum of all areas is 280 sq in. Which is less than 340, but more than 225. But putting all that aside, I want to focus only on the ratios. Before the change, 3 sets of rooms each got somewhere in the ballpark of 100 sq in. Now after the change, there are only 2 sets of rooms, which makes me worry if the set getting 184 (i.e. the set supplied by the 2 supply ducts that were combined) is either (a) not getting enough air or (b) getting air that is moving too fast and is either loud or problematic for some other reason. I found some cheap wireless temp sensors and have been tracking the temp of every room. Somewhat surprisingly, the TV room gets the most heat (it is winter where I am), despite being in the possibly undersupplied group. But also the TV room has TWO large vents. Probably the only rooms that seem to be maybe not getting enough air (i.e. are a few degrees colder than the others) are the office and family room. These ARE in the undersupplied group, but they're also smaller vents in general. I have no idea what to conclude from all of this, but I think I still am inclined to ask the installer to connect the 3rd downstairs 12\" duct directly back to the plenum, rather than its current position of joined with a sister duct. This would increase the overall air capacity coming out of the plenum. I'm curious what the pros think about this. Thanks!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/3df2d71401cc2733_9334-w500-h740-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c852f8c601cc2736_9334-w500-h203-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

main_question: {"author_id": "moosemac-gw", "author_name": "moosemac", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/moosemac-gw", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "This isn't PC but I need to vent. DD had an oncologist appointment Monday morning. The doctor found a lump in her left breast which he believes is a lump that had been previously biopsied. However, it raised enough concern that he wanted her to have a mammogram and an ultrasound. Her oncologist is affiliated with a large Boston hospital. The staff at the local cancer center always arranges the appointments for their patients. After 2+ days of calling, the appointment coordinator called DD today and relayed the following story: The coordinator had called every hospital in their network and the earliest appointment would be for some time in February. The coordinator then informed the oncologist who said that was unacceptable as DD has a very aggressive form of beast cancer which up to this point has been in remission. The oncologist and a colleague ended up making calls, calling in favors and were able to get DD an appointment today. I shudder to think what could happen if the lump is cancer and DD had to wait until February. The reason I am so perturbed is in talking to numerous nurse friends who work in various areas of the hospitals and cancer center, everyone has told me the same story. The hospitals are not overwhelmed by patients\u2019 sick from COVID but rather they are overwhelmed by patients with coping issues who are flooding the ER\u2019s. Many of these patients once in the ER are tested for COVID and are positive but asymptomatic thus the COVID numbers for the hospitals appear high. There are so many of these cases that the hospitals are being forced to shift resources from other departments to handle the case load. This begs a deeper question: What happened to society and self-resilience? I understand there are genuine mental health issues and those are serious but why is there a general lack of coping skills in entire generations? Our parents, grandparents and ancestors went through crisis of similar magnitude or worse than the COVID and they coped without running to the ER. What changed? Better yet, how do we fix the problem? title: Putting Away Your Holiday Decor | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "internet1382", "author_name": "Aphaea", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/internet1382", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "Please share what you are doing or have done this year as regards putting away and/or getting rid of any holiday decorations for Halloween, autumn, Thanksgiving, Hanukkah or Christmas. Did you decide to get rid of things? If so, what were they and why did you choose them? Did you give them away before the holiday or after?  What about what you are keeping?  How do you pack it? Where do you keep it? Is it organized and if so, how? What kind of storage do you use?  Where will it reside until you use it again? Do you buy organizers or use boxes/bags? Got any secrets or tips you are willing to share? I got three younger cats in late summer as my other three died of old age earlier. I had forgotten what  younger means--lots of play, destructive behaviors during said play, insatiable curiosity. I had given my lipstick red Christmas tree (and its gorgeous antique and vintage ornaments) to my favorite thrift store because my new home is green and white and I wanted to go with those calming and peaceful colors. It turned out to be a good thing because the cats' destructive play would probably have meant the end of it. I was a bit sad I couldn't have my late mother's small Hallmark cardboard antique stove (with turkey in oven) out for the autumn season but I wanted it to live teethmark-free for many more years. I used two tabletop flocked trees, carefully, but the cats didn't care about them at all. They did however take an interest in a small miniature forest I have but that seemed to wear off over time. All in all, not too bad. I was able to cut my autumn decorations to about half of the strong cardboard Chewy shipping  boxes I use because of not putting all the faux pumpkins in smaller individual boxes. They are protected from one other by squares of small bubble wrap. And since no one but me will touch them I am not worried about they getting damaged. I love seeing maybe three or four medium-sized boxes and know that next year will be even easier to set them up and take them down. Now I am beginning to prepare the Christmas items for storage. Again, I am going to try to cut down by about half.  Since it is after Christmas I will designate one box for all items that I think I might get rid of by donating them to the thrift store in September. It will be well marked and easy to get to at that time. Plus, I made the decision that I am not going to buy a six-foot tree; I will stick with three flocked tabletop trees and a tiny six-inch gold tree. None will have lights or ornaments. I ended up not doing that this year and it turns out I love it. I used a real TJ's wreath on the door and will do that again. It's easier than storing a faux one and it smells wonderful. (Alas, all real decorations have to go on the porch; can't take the risk with the cats.) The  didn't get tied onto a pretty jute rope this year but that was okay; they decorated the coffee table.  In the meantime, I will keep an eye out at the thrift store and elsewhere for those plastic storage boxes with locking lids. Sturdy as the Chewy boxes are I want to get everything into those bins eventually. This year's celebrations, partly due to COVID and partly to my own choice to scale down and concentrate on what I own and love (and not to buy) has made not just the holiday easier and truly more memorable and valuable, but I am finding joy in packing them up as well. And when I finish that part I will begin my January ritual,  Apartment Therapy's January Cure.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/068252e001ccae3a_3898-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

main_question: {"author_id": "henry-kuska0", "author_name": "Henry Kuska", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/henry-kuska0", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "Abstract: \"Pomegranate (Punica granatum L.) fruit peel (PFPAE) aqueous extract was evaluated for the possible control of common sucking pests of roses viz., aphids (Macrosiphum roseiformis Davis), thrips (Scirthothrips dorsalis Hood) and two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae Koch). Toxicity bioassays were done with both leaf dip and potted plant treatment and compared with positive control (imidacloprid and spiromesifen). main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-8264262", "author_name": "Gwen Hobson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-8264262", "date": "2021-12-29", "text": "gwenyhobbs@icloud.com", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/3661c39e01cbc3e3_6686-w500-h374-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "zen-cabinetry-pfvwus-pf~755207933", "author_name": "Zen Cabinetry", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/zen-cabinetry-pfvwus-pf~755207933", "date": "2022-01-06", "text": "I would prepare a basic plan in which it includes basic length, width and ceiling height dimensions of current bathroom, the idea of what kind of shower, vanity, and tiles would like, and range of materials would be used. It was the mid-1970s, and the place was decorated in a very casual, naturally hippy style. Artsy textiles and prints, sprawling plants everywhere, macrame, great rock and folk music playing. I loved it. And I really loved the fried eggplant. Anyway \u2026 There was an art print on the wall that my dad and I were mesmerized by. We\u2019d always study it, wondering what in the world it represented. It certainly wasn\u2019t like our decor at home, but we loved it, and over the years would sit at the table nearest it, like visiting an old friend. Eventually that location closed, but the original in Fort Worth stayed open. I kind of forgot it was there and rarely went. When I did, I wondered what happened to the strange Granger poster. Fast forward \u2026 my DH moves here from LI, and as we drove by Zeke\u2019s one day, I said hey, you need to try this place. We go in. Still old decor. Still same menu. You order at the counter as soon as you step in the door. We go on through to the dining section, and \u2026. no way. The Granger poster is on the wall!! I nearly cheered out loud, and told DH why I was so excited. He agreed it was very interesting and compelling. The tradition started again \u2014 go to Zeke\u2019s, enjoy lunch, visit the Granger. Well, last time we went, it was gone. No one knew where it went. The founder is still running the place, but wasn\u2019t there. Maybe he took it home, or sold it, or something? I decided one day to look it up, just to try to save a picture so I wouldn\u2019t forget it. I discovered not many images of it exist. But then \u2026 I see one for sale on Ebay! I bid, it\u2019s rejected. Bid again, rejected. Bid one more time \u2014 MINE. And it gets here today! I called my dad and he was so excited. He said he loved watching me looking at it as a kid, and how we\u2019d muse about it. If you made it this far, thanks for reading. Here it is. main_question: {"author_id": "zeek-bird", "author_name": "scout", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/zeek-bird", "date": "2021-12-30", "text": "I live in a state with very hard water.   Any recommendations for a water softener?   I have a large house if that makes a difference.   My newly installed shower tile (dark blue) has water stains.   Luckily I used white tiles for the rest of the bathrooms.  The fixtures accumulate hard water droplets.  The faucets get clogged with calcium debris. Also, can soft water be drunk? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2021-12-31", "text": "\"I will make sure to stress this as I look for it.\" Water softeners all work the same way. They replace hardness ions (calcium and magnesium) with sodium ions from the salt.  Thus, the level of sodium in soft water is = to the amount in the water in the first place + the amount of hardness. No water softener produces more \"drinkable\" water than another. Soft water is fine for humans. There are some people on a very low sodium diet who are advised not to drink soft water. I have very hard water (24 gpg) and when I drink softened water it tastes fine. That said, small animals and fish may be more sensitive to the slightly elevated sodium levels in the same way fish are to chlorine in municipal tap water. Plumb a faucet in the kitchen with unsoftened water. My cold water in the kitchen is filtered (removes chlorine, taste, odor, and many chemicals) but isn't softened. This is what I use to cook with, water indoor plants, put in the dog bowl. This is a common setup with soft water.", "images": []}}

We are in central Wisconsin. What I would like to know is do dwarf and/or semi-dwarf trees produce faster (i.e. in less number of years for the first production) than standard sized trees? Other than size, are there any other advantages/disadvantages of one over the other? Thank you.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "johnfduda", "author_name": "John D Zn6a PIT Pa", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/johnfduda", "date": "2021-12-30", "text": "Generally the smaller the rootstock the faster the tree will produce it's first fruit.However it's been said that after the first couple years the bigger tree will produce more fruit than the smaller in any one of the following years. Some of the larger rootstocks will not tend to blow down as they root better especially in poor soil like clay, An apple rootstock like MM111 which some call a semi full size will grow as a semi dwarf in colder climates or poorer soils. That one also is said to not need staking in most places. Many sources of trees won't tell you what rootstock you selection is on. One that does is Fedco Trees from Maine who sells to customers in Zones as cold as USDA 3. There are also differences from one rootstock to another in resistance to tree diseases such as fireblight. Cummins Nursery from upstate NY has some discussion on a larger choice of rootstocks. You should also know that there are big differences in growth between varieties of the same fruit. Take Honeycrisp called a low vigor tree by Fedco. I've seen differences among varieties of the same apple variety. Red Delicious and Mcintosh have large differences among different sports. So you could adjust the rootstock size according to the varieties of the same fruit to get a similar size tree.", "images": []}}

We're very excited for this new journey, but I don't know what to do about announcing our new home and housewarming. I'm getting all sorts of different advice from my Mom, MIL, aunt, sister, and friends. The varying advice has me confused on what to do, so thought I'd come here to ask for help! We moved to a new state right before the pandemic, this is the state where we've purchased our new home. Since we moved here before the pandemic, we haven't had much opportunity to make new friends and our existing friends and family all live out of state, so having an actual in-person housewarming seems inappropriate to me since it would require everyone to travel quite a distance. Not to mention it seems a bit irresponsible to have a big party with the continuation of the Coronavirus. Because of this... My mom and sister suggested we mail out \"new home\" announcements to our family and close friends. This, I am completely okay with! On the announcement, I'd like to make a point of letting everyone know they're welcome to visit us and we'd love to host them. However, other family members have suggested including a \"housewarming registry\" on our announcements since we can't have an actual in-person housewarming party. I don't know how to feel about this. Housewarming gifts would obviously be nice since we're stretched a bit thin, but I also don't want to make family and friends feel obligated or awkward about sending us a gift. Not to mention the pandemic has taken a financial toll on everyone, so to ask for gifts during this time seems wrong. But I don't know... maybe it's common to include a registry? title: Need help eliminating condensation from basement walls with poly. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "cory-hauser", "author_name": "Cory Hauser", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cory-hauser", "date": "2021-12-31", "text": "Climate Zone 5A (Eastern Nebraska) I\u2019m needing guidance on properly insulating basement walls that already have 6 mil poly fastened to the wall as part of a basement perimeter drain system. I recently noticed condensation on the warm side of the 6 mil poly (not between the poly and poured concrete wall) and am unsure how to proceed. (basement humidity is around 50%, basement air temp around 63 degrees F, outside temp is currently 20 degrees F) Over the summer I installed a basement perimeter drain like in the attached picture. As part of the system, I covered the walls in 6 mil poly. The 6 mil poly is tucked inside the dimple mat at the bottom and then mechanically fastened at the top with Christmas tree fasteners. I then sealed the top of the 6 mil poly with a sealant and taped the bottom of the 6 mil poly to the dimple mat. This system has been in place for 6 months and appears to have taken care of my damp basement. However, I recently started to finish my basement. Since I had the 6 mil poly on top of the poured concrete walls, I made the incorrect assumption that I could simply put in fiberglass batt insulation within my 2\u00d74 cavities. Only after getting all of my drywall up did I notice condensation on the warm side of the 6 mil poly (not between the poly and poured concrete wall). The condensation is only on the top 1 foot of my poly with no current signs of condensation below that. main_question: {"author_id": "fantim", "author_name": "fantim", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fantim", "date": "2021-12-31", "text": "We are completely renovating a row house built between 1890 and 1900, starting with the ground floor (we have tenants on the second floor at the moment).The staircase going from the ground floor to the second floor is a winder type stair and it is sagging by about 1 - 11/2 inches. We were thinking of straightening it by shimming the bottom up and tightening the stringers together (using turnbuckles), and then somehow reattaching the newel post that detached itself from the stringer and the angled steps.Another option was to simply strengthen the stairs and leave them crooked by sistering the joist below and adding blocking to the threads and risers.The stringers rest on an angled landing joist at the bottom that either sagged by 1 inch or was installed crooked. This joist is damaged and needs help. All the surrounding joists are straight. All of the risers are sitting on the mortise of the outer stringer by about 1/4 inch, except for one that completely fell out.The inner stringer seems to be attached to the brick.We are not completely sure how the staircase holds at the top, but we can see the newel post detached itself from the stringer and some of the angled steps.Any thoughts or ideas on how we can tackle these problems?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b3b2bba301cf1af3_2808-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a2f2b05801cf1af5_2811-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6552983e01cf1af8_2816-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2552905e01cf1afa_2817-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

Inspectors tend to be far stricter when inspecting rental property (a homeowner can't pull a permit on multi family housing in my state).", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "weedyacres", "author_name": "weedyacres", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/weedyacres", "date": "2022-01-04", "text": "I'd say you need to start by making solid top and bottom supports for the stringers.  If they are on solid footing, and plumb/level/square, then the rest can fall into place.   So you've just got 2 stringers, one on either side, and then some sort of wonky strips on the underside of the stairs that were tied into the post with the ? on it? title: How did you compare builders? What drove your decision? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-29405466", "author_name": "2rickies", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-29405466", "date": "2021-12-31", "text": "What to you, is the most important consideration when choosing a builder? As I talk with builders and try to make a decision, of course I'm considering the quality of their work first. Then I'm comparing their job management structure. And, I'm trying to educate myself about the contract types--cost-plus, fixed price, and variations on those themes. Our architect favors fixed price, says all the projects he does, even now, are under that type of contract, so I went into this assuming that fixed price was what we wanted, but I'm not sure now. The smallest local builders use cost-plus and always have. The slightly larger builders offer more flexibility, but have (understandably) added materials escalation clauses to their contracts, essentially changing a fixed contract into a cost-plus. I'm wary of cost-plus because even though it's more transparent, it feels so open-ended. I've been thinking that cost plus with a guaranteed maximum, where if we come under we split the difference with the builder, might be the way to go. But I wonder if that will be hard to get in the current market. That brings me to two builders I'm attempting to compare. Both of these builders come highly recommended.
